title: Are VLMs Seeing or Just Saying? Uncovering the Illusion of Visual Re-examination
one_liner: VISUALSWAP tests whether a vision-language model truly looks back at the image during reasoning by swapping in a similar-looking but semantically different image midstream and checking whether the model notices.
lead: Many vision-language models produce reasoning traces that say things such as 'let me check the figure again.' The paper asks whether those statements correspond to an actual second use of the image or whether they are only familiar text patterns produced during generation. VISUALSWAP probes that question directly. After the model has started reasoning over one image, the benchmark silently replaces that image with a visually similar but semantically different image and checks whether the model's answer changes or whether it notices the mismatch. If the model truly re-examines the image, it should react to the swap because the visual evidence has changed. If it continues the same reasoning trace, the self-reflective language was only text. The paper matters because it separates verbal claims of re-checking from measurable re-grounding in the visual input.

problem.h2: Why a reasoning trace can be misleading
paras: A model can generate a convincing chain of text without actually using new visual evidence at each step. Once a reasoning trace is underway, the model may simply continue from its own previous text because that continuation is statistically likely under its language model. In that case, phrases about checking the image again say nothing about whether the visual branch was consulted.

Standard accuracy benchmarks miss this distinction because they only score the final answer. A model can answer correctly on many examples while still failing to revisit the image when its own reasoning claims that it did. The paper therefore designs a causal probe: change the image after the reasoning has begun and observe whether the model's internal dependence on visual input is real.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Swap the image mid-reasoning and test whether the model's subsequent behavior reflects the new visual evidence or only its earlier text continuation.

paras: The paper changes the evaluation protocol. Instead of trusting self-reflective text at face value, it intervenes on the image during generation and tests whether the model's later computation remains causally tied to visual evidence.
object.object: the benchmark used to evaluate visual re-examination

hidden.name: actual visual re-grounding during generation
paras: The hidden quantity is whether later generated output positions are conditioned on the current image or mostly on the model's own earlier text. That dependence is not visible from the text alone because the same phrase about checking the image can appear in both grounded and ungrounded traces.

VISUALSWAP estimates this hidden dependence by intervention. If changing the image changes the later answer or causes the model to detect inconsistency, then later computation still depends on visual evidence. If the output barely changes, the dependence is weak even when the text claims otherwise.

heat.caption: The benchmark isolates whether later output positions remain anchored to the changed image or drift into text-only continuation.

reads.html: The paper is measuring whether the model really looks again when it says it is looking again.
VISUALSWAP probes causal visual grounding by intervening on the image after reasoning begins and observing whether subsequent generation responds to the new image-derived inputs.

mechanism.h2: Why the image-swap probe is decisive
paras: The probe works because it changes only the visual evidence while leaving the earlier text trace intact. If later reasoning is grounded in the image, the model now faces a conflict between its previous partial explanation and the new picture. Resolving that conflict requires detecting the swap, revising the answer, or at least shifting focus back to the image-derived inputs.

If the model instead continues almost unchanged, the simplest explanation is that generation after the swap is driven mainly by text inertia, meaning the tendency to continue the existing answer pattern. In that regime, self-reflective phrases are weak evidence of perception because the language branch can emit them without reopening the visual branch in a way that changes the computation.

Focus-pattern analysis strengthens the conclusion. The paper reports that explicit user instructions to re-check can increase focus weight on image-derived inputs, while self-generated reflection often does not. That difference matters because it shows the failure is not that the model can never revisit the image. The failure is that spontaneous reflective language does not reliably trigger the visual re-grounding that the language suggests.

stages.s: Swap in a similar-looking but semantically different image
Observe later answer and image-focus weights
Estimate whether the model actually re-grounded in the new image

math.words: A model shows visual re-grounding when its post-swap behavior differs in the direction implied by the replacement image, and the benchmark can summarize that with swap-sensitive accuracy and detection metrics.
symbols: the fraction of swapped examples where the model reacts appropriately after the image change
cases where the model either updates to the new correct answer or explicitly notices the inconsistency
the number of examples evaluated under image replacement

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose image A contains a triangle and image B contains a square in the answer-relevant region.
The model begins reasoning on image A and states that the shape appears triangular.
VISUALSWAP replaces image A with image B before the model finishes.
If the model truly re-examines the image, it should revise the answer toward square or report a mismatch.
If it keeps the triangle answer, the swap reveals that later output positions depended mostly on the earlier text trace rather than the current image.

math.note: The metric is simple on purpose: the benchmark wants a behavioral readout of grounding after intervention, not a subjective judgment of the reasoning style.

charts.title: Self-reflective reasoning trace alone
charts.note: Reflective language by itself is weak evidence because the model can continue the trace even after the image has changed.

charts.title: Explicit user prompt to re-check
charts.note: Direct instructions can improve grounding because they raise the chance that computation returns to the image-derived inputs. The values are illustrative summaries of the reported trend.

items.b: Swap pairs can be too easy or too hard.
items.html: If the swapped images differ in obvious low-level ways, the benchmark may overestimate re-grounding because noticing the change becomes trivial. If they are nearly indistinguishable, the benchmark may underestimate it because even a grounded model lacks enough evidence.

If generation stops too early, the model may not have enough opportunity to react after the swap, which weakens the causal test because the intervention arrives too late to affect many later output positions.

items.b: Focus weights are only one diagnostic.
items.html: A rise in focus weight on image-derived inputs helps interpret the behavior, but that signal alone does not prove correct use of the image because the model can look back without extracting the needed semantics.
The benchmark is strongest when paired images are semantically different in answer-relevant ways but still visually close enough that simple mismatch cues do not dominate.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small benchmark of paired images where each pair differs in one answer-critical detail, such as the chart value, geometric shape, or count of objects. Run a vision-language model in two conditions: normal generation and generation with a midstream image swap. Also run a third condition where the user explicitly instructs the model to re-check after the swap.

Track answer changes, swap detection, and image-focus weights after the intervention. The demo should prove that reflective phrases alone do not guarantee renewed visual grounding, because the decisive evidence is whether the model reacts to the changed image.
demo.closing: The demo must make the causal distinction clear: the question is not whether the model can say it is checking, but whether changing the image changes what it does next.
